messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir's life changed forever on a fateful night when he was sexually assaulted by a man in authority. The memories of that event still lingered vividly in his mind, but it was the sounds that haunted him the most - the sirens blaring outside, the commotion, and the feeling of being completely powerless. Even now, whenever Amir heard sirens or saw ambulances rushing to an emergency, he would feel a chill run down his spine, instantly transporting him back to that night. As time passed, Amir began to develop strategies to cope with these triggers. He started avoiding places where he might encounter men in uniform or see ambulances, such as hospitals or areas near police stations. He even took detours on his daily commute to work as a software engineer to steer clear of the place where the assault occurred. Amir felt that by controlling his environment, he could minimize the chances of being confronted with these distressing reminders. However, this avoidance also meant that he was restricting himself to a narrow "safe zone" - a limited number of places where he felt comfortable and secure. But despite his best efforts, Amir couldn't shake off the feeling of being constantly on edge. He often found himself scanning his surroundings for potential signs of danger, even when there were none. His friends and family noticed that he would become easily agitated or irritable in situations that didn't seem to warrant such a strong reaction. Amir's internal narrative had convinced him that the world was a treacherous place, full of hidden threats waiting to pounce. This hypervigilance was closely tied to his deep-seated feelings of injustice and self-blame. Amir couldn't understand why he had been targeted by someone in authority, and why nothing seemed to have been done about it. He began to wonder if he had somehow brought this upon himself through his actions or behavior that night. These negative appraisals reinforced his avoidance behaviors - if he felt responsible for the assault, then maybe he could prevent future incidents by controlling his environment. As Amir navigated his daily life, these maladaptive strategies started to reinforce each other in a vicious cycle. His avoidance of authority figures and uniforms made him even more anxious around people in power, which in turn fueled his constant scanning for danger. This hyperarousal state then heightened his reaction to sirens or ambulances, making it even harder for him to venture out into the world. Amir's self-imposed isolation also meant that he was giving up things he once enjoyed, like socializing with friends or exploring new places. His job as a software engineer began to suffer as well, as his constant anxiety made it difficult for him to focus on complex projects. He felt trapped in this narrow existence, unable to break free from the cycle of fear and avoidance. Despite everything, Amir held onto one last hope - that he could find some way to heal and move forward. It was this glimmer of resilience that finally brought him to seek help, hoping that a therapist might be able to guide him out of this dark labyrinth and back into a life filled with purpose and meaning.
